# tasks

<!-- ops:identity start — generated by ops-docs; edit identity.toml -->
Tracks a project's work as one markdown file per task, checked into the project, for
coding agents and the people supervising them. A single Rust binary is the only writer
and answers in JSON by default; the skills shipped beside it teach agents the session
protocol. Each host registers its projects, so one command can read across all of them.

Authority: `docs/specs/2026-08-29-tasks-design.md`
<!-- ops:identity end -->

This README runs from [setup](#setup) and [usage](#usage) through the
[concepts](#concepts) to a [reference](#reference) section per feature, each with its
design link.

## Setup

<a id="quick-start"></a>

If you are an agent asked to install `tasks` or adopt it in a project, do steps 1–3 in
order. Each step is idempotent.

### 1. Install

Install the binary and the skill (once per machine; needs a Rust toolchain):

    git clone https://github.com/khughitt/tasks ~/.local/src/tasks
    cargo install --locked --path ~/.local/src/tasks
    just --justfile ~/.local/src/tasks/justfile install-skills

`--locked` installs the checked dependency versions; from a checkout you already have,
`cargo install --locked --path .` does the same. `install-skills` symlinks every
`skills/*` directory into `~/.claude/skills` and `~/.agents/skills` (the latter for other
harnesses). Without `just`:
`ln -sfn ~/.local/src/tasks/skills/tasks ~/.claude/skills/tasks`.

Without a checkout (binary only; the skill still needs the `skills/tasks` directory
from a clone):

    cargo install --git https://github.com/khughitt/tasks

See [Agent skills](#agent-skills) for a per-project copy and the other skills.

### 2. Initialize a project

Once per repository:

    cd <repo>
    tasks init --prefix <p>          # p: a letter then 1-7 letters/digits, e.g. sci

`init` creates `tasks/` and the doc roots and registers the project. If the project keeps
specs or plans outside `docs/specs/` and `docs/plans/`, see
[Adopting in an existing project](#adopting-in-an-existing-project) before running `init`.

### 3. Tell the project's agents

Add this to the project's `AGENTS.md` or `CLAUDE.md`:

    Work is tracked with `tasks` (see ~/.claude/skills/tasks/SKILL.md). Start every
    session with `tasks prime`, `tasks start <id>` before changing code, `tasks done <id>`
    on the task's branch before it merges, and `tasks check` before every commit.

    Adopt the process and workspace policy in the tasks skill: the task's process
    field, not generic Superpowers triggers, decides whether brainstorming runs.
    Direct executes scoped work without brainstorming or new design/plan documents;
    planned requires user review of a written spec, then a written implementation
    plan, before implementation. Assess missing process explicitly before coding.
    Both code paths use an isolated task worktree, reusing one on resume or creating
    one with git worktree add under .worktrees/; run just setup when defined.
    Planned work creates it before drafting the spec. Explicit user overrides win.

## Usage

Add a task and work it:

    tasks add "Emit rows" -p 1 --size s --complexity low --process direct
    tasks prime                      # counts, lanes, ready list, who is doing what
    tasks ready                      # what can be worked on now
    tasks tree                       # the goal hierarchy
    tasks start <id>                 # claim it
    tasks note <id> "<one line>"     # when scope or understanding changes
    tasks park <id> "<next step>"    # set it down; start resumes it
    tasks done <id> "<what landed>"  # on the task's branch before it merges
    tasks check                      # before every commit
    tasks feedback --project tasks "<about the tool>" --category friction   # file friction with this tool

Never edit `tasks/*.md` by hand. Add `--pretty` to any command for human-readable
output. The [command tour](#command-tour) shows the rest of the CLI, and
[Output and errors](#output-and-errors) covers help, exit codes and the JSON contract.

## Layout

What `tasks` writes in a project and on each host:

    tasks/.config.toml               prefix = "sci"; optional color / spec_dirs / plan_dirs / [tags] / [git]
    tasks/sci-4f2a9c.md              one task
    tasks/files/sci-4f2a9c/          the task's attachments
    ~/.config/tasks/projects.toml    per-machine registry: live prefix -> repo path; retired -> live; [records] prefix -> records dir; [groups] name -> prefixes
    ~/.local/state/tasks/            per-machine state ($XDG_STATE_HOME): claims and parks, move and rename journals, record-commit locks

This repository:

    src/                             the CLI: parser, one module per subcommand, the record model
    tests/                           end-to-end tests against the built binary in temp repos
    skills/                          the tasks, curate and scope agent skills
    docs/specs/, docs/plans/         design and plan documents, linked from tasks
    tools/                           tt, ops-check, ops-docs and cli.toml vendored from ops (tools/README.md); review and wait backfills

## Consumers

Every project registered on these hosts tracks its work with `tasks` and loads the
skills in `skills/`. [tasks-tui](https://github.com/khughitt/tasks-tui) (`tui`) is a
terminal front end: it shells out to `tasks`, reads the JSON, and launches an agent on a
task in a new terminal. The CLI is the whole contract; the TUI never touches
`tasks/*.md`. `obs` indexes task records and parses the note shapes its outcome
measures read; lookout (`look`) shows task state beside live agents; `flows` keeps each
flow's state and gate evidence in task notes; `crew` reads tasks as work items; and `ops`
reads the host registry to join each project's declared identity to its registered root.

## Concepts

### Statuses

Statuses are `idea`, `todo`, `doing`, `blocked`, `shelved`, `done`, and `dropped`, plus
`moved`, the read-only tombstone [`tasks move`](#moving-tasks) leaves behind.
An idea is an uncommitted thought and is never offered by `ready`; scope it into a `todo`
first ([From idea to ready work](#from-idea-to-ready-work)). `shelved` is open but hidden; use `tasks shelve <id> "<wake condition>"` and
`tasks unshelve <id>` to return it as an idea.

Ideas carry an optional `reviewed` flag (set by `note --reviewed` and `edit --reviewed`,
which also stamp `reviewed_at`; cleared by `--no-reviewed` and by every status change),
and an `awaiting_user` marker for a reviewed idea waiting on the user. Every close to
done or dropped stamps `closed`. Summary rows carry a derived `needs_review` and its
`review_reason` (`unreviewed`, `woken`, `stranded`, `unassessed`): a reviewed idea needs
review again when it waits on nothing recorded. `--needs-review` filters on it and
pretty tables mark it with `*`. Older binaries cannot parse records carrying `reviewed`,
`awaiting_user`, `reviewed_at` or `closed`: update every host reading synced tasks
before any of them runs this version, since every `done` and `drop` writes `closed`.

`--defer <date|Nd|Nw>` hides a task from the pickers until the date; any status change
clears it. A recurring task (`--every`) closes normally: `done` records the completion
and anchors its next cycle. When due, it appears in `ready` with status `done`; use
`start` before completing the next occurrence. Early runs are allowed. `--every` accepts
positive whole days or weeks (for example, `30d` or `2w`), up to 36500 days; goals
cannot recur.

### From idea to ready work

Work usually enters as an idea and reaches `ready` through one or more `/scope` passes.
This is the shape of that path across sessions; the
[scope skill](skills/scope/SKILL.md) holds the procedure.

1. **Capture.** `tasks add "<title>" --status idea` records a thought without committing
   to it.
2. **Scope.** `/scope` reviews a small cluster of ideas against evidence (code, history,
   sources, linked work) and gives each one verdict: `scoped` promotes it to `todo` with
   a body saying why, what done means and where to look, rated and with its process
   chosen; the others are `briefed`, `question` (only the user can answer), `shelved`,
   or a proposed drop. Scoping weighs evidence; it does not do the research or the work.
3. **Brief and research.** When decisions remain, the pass writes a one-page brief under
   `docs/notes/` framing the alternatives and unanswered questions, and the idea stays an
   idea. Each bounded question the brief needs answered becomes an ordinary task (its
   question, where to start, a bound, the expected result and the ideas it wakes), or a
   design task when the questions need design; the waiting ideas depend on it.
4. **Do the research.** There is no research command: a research task is ready work like
   any other, picked through `tasks ready` or `tasks next` and taken with `tasks start`.
   Its completion adds the finding to each waiting idea with
   `tasks note <id> --no-reviewed "<finding>"`; an answer to a `question` is recorded the
   same way.
5. **Scope again.** Closing the research clears the dependency, so the idea returns to the
   review queue (`woken`, or `unreviewed` once a finding is noted). The next `/scope`
   picks it up and reuses the existing brief, goal and research tasks rather than
   starting over.
6. **Re-scope before building.** When a `todo` or `blocked` task's premises change,
   `/scope <id>` re-checks them before implementation: it narrows the task, confirms it,
   or returns it to `idea` when a decision has reopened.

Scoping settles what the work is, not how it is reviewed: a scoped `direct` task runs
from its body, while `planned` work still needs its reviewed design spec and
implementation plan ([Process](#process)).

### Goals, lanes and dependencies

A task with children is a goal: `tasks add "<piece>" --parent <goal>` decomposes it,
and `ready` and `next` never offer it. `done` refuses while any descendant is open
(`--force` overrides); `drop` refuses too, with no override. `prime`'s closeout lists
goals whose work is all done, to confirm and close. A parent must be in the same project.

`depends` orders work: `ready` offers a task only once all its dependencies are closed.
`edit --depends` adds one, and `tasks dep <id> --on <x> --rm <y>` swaps one in a single
save. A dependency may name a task in another registered project, so a goal whose pieces
live elsewhere holds them as dependencies.

A lane (`add --lane`) is a goal for an effort meant to run beside the project's other
efforts. The first paragraph of its body is its guidance in `prime` and `tasks lanes`;
`next --under <lane>` picks within it, and `tasks block <lane> "<why>"` pauses its
subtree until `tasks unblock`. A lane cannot nest inside a lane.

A need (`--need <name>`, declared under `[needs]` in `tasks/.config.toml`) names a shared
resource a step uses. An exclusive need serves one session at a time; see [Claims](#claims).

### Blockers

`tasks blockers` ranks the open prerequisites holding up the most open work (design:
`docs/specs/2026-10-25-blocker-ranking-design.md`). It reads one scan and writes nothing;
`ready` and `next` keep their order. Each row counts the open records that depend on it
directly and through chains of `depends`, each once. Ideas, blocked, deferred and
shelved records count as affected work, and goals are counted separately. Rows rank by
transitive work, then direct work, the row's own declared priority, creation time and
id. `--limit` (`-n`; default 20, `0` for totals and coverage only) truncates after ranking.

- **Scope.** Dependents are counted in the current project by default, or under
  `--project`, `--group` or `--all-projects`. A prerequisite in another project still gets a
  row, but its own dependencies are not followed: `coverage.unfollowed_targets` names
  it, and `coverage.complete` is false. A missing, unregistered or move-looping reference
  is listed under `unresolved` and also makes the scan partial. An unreachable project
  does too. A partial scan's counts are lower bounds and its ranks are observed ranks;
  `--all-projects` follows the paths a narrower scope cut.
- **What a count is not.** `dependencies_cleared_direct_count` counts direct dependents
  whose every other dependency is already satisfied. It is not readiness or
  permission: lifecycle, deferrals, claims, needs and approvals still apply. Goals are
  structural only (lanes and records with children). A childless closeout hub whose
  purpose lives in prose counts as work, and a goal's children get none of its impact
  without an explicit dependency.
- **Whose move it is.** `attention` is `user` only on recorded evidence: a park waiting on
  the user (`--waiting-on user`, with its reason and next step), or a reviewed idea marked
  `--awaiting-user`. Everything else is `unknown`, including an approval gate written
  only in a body: record it with `tasks park <id> "<step>" --waiting-on user --reason
  approval` before the report can show it. Parks and claims are this host's evidence
  (`park_evidence.host`), so a park recorded on another host is unknown here. A declared
  need (`task_needs`) names a resource, not an approval; a park's own `needs` is its host
  requirement.
- **Not yet measured.** How long a prerequisite has blocked, and across how many scope
  passes, is not recorded yet; the report says so in its warnings and does not estimate it.

### Process

Every task can record how an agent works it. `--process direct|planned` on `add` or
`edit` chooses; [Choosing a process](#choosing-a-process) is the full policy.

| Process | Agent workflow |
|---------|----------------|
| `direct` | Execute the scoped task or reviewed plan without brainstorming or new design/plan documents. |
| `planned` | Review a written design spec with the user, then review a written implementation plan, before implementing. |
| Unassessed | Read the task and relevant code, explicitly record the choice and its reason before implementation. |

### Parks

`park` sets a task down with its next step in the same store, who it waits on, and
optionally why:

| reason        | The work stopped because…                                                        |
|---------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `review`      | an artifact the user must inspect and judge: art sheets, screenshots, a document read |
| `decision`    | a decision only the user can make — scope, taste, priority                       |
| `approval`    | the agent holds a recommendation and wants it confirmed                          |
| `environment` | the checkout or machine cannot run the work — missing deps, a restart, a TTY     |
| `dependency`  | another task or project must land first                                          |
| `session`     | the session ended before the work did — context exhausted, time, crash           |
| `capability`  | the work needs more reasoning than this session can supply; `--complexity` raises the rating |
| `quiet`       | the host is in use; the work is prepared, unattended, and needs only an idle machine — `--minutes <n>` (required) and `--needs idle\|headless` record the recipe |

`start` resumes it, and `prime` lists parked work first. Parks are host-local, so a park
can outlive a close made on another host or checkout; `prime` reports such a park as a
warning naming the command that clears it (repeating the close) rather than as a row,
while `list --parked` omits it unless given a status filter. Every record also carries two
stamps written only by status changes: `started`, the first time work began, and
`completed`, the latest completion (cleared by a reopen). Design:
`docs/specs/2026-09-11-park-reason-and-stamps-design.md`.

`tasks quiet` lists quiet parks across every registered project as resume briefs (design:
`docs/specs/2026-09-13-quiet-queue-design.md`); the ordinary pretty tables (`list`,
`prime`, `ready`) mark a quiet park's row with its recipe, such as
`waits on user, quiet; idle, 40 min`. A quiet park's next step lists the run's
phases and any refusal or hang an earlier attempt of the recipe hit. Every attempt then ends
with one note in a fixed form, so the estimate can be compared with what happened:

    run: <actual> min (est <n>, <needs>); <phase> <m>, …; <outcome>[: <cause>]

`<outcome>` is `passed`, `failed`, `refused`, `hung`, or `aborted`. A refused attempt is
timed up to the refusal and gets its note too.

<a id="claims-and-checkouts"></a>

### Claims

`start` also writes a per-project claim outside git, so every worktree sees the session and
its liveness. `ready` and `next` omit live claims with an explanatory warning. When concrete native identity is unavailable, set
`TASKS_SESSION` per agent sharing a terminal or harness process; use
`tasks start --force <id>` for an explicit, recorded takeover. A write refuses with
`stale_copy` when another worktree holds a newer copy of the record, and says whether to
rerun there, merge, or leave it to the session working there.
An open `halt` task in the registered checkout blocks new lower-priority starts across
worktrees. `prime`, `ready`, and `next` show the halt and eligible work. An audited
override is `tasks start <id> --force --reason "<one-line explanation>"`; its free-text
reason is recorded on the halt and target, unlike park's fixed-list `--reason`.

An exclusive need (`exclusive = true` under `[needs]`) is held by the live claim of the
task that needs it, across every registered project on the host. Other sessions' steps
that need it leave `ready`, `next` and `prime` with a warning naming the holder, and `start`
refuses them with `need_held`. `tasks start <id> --force --reason "…"` overrides with a
note on the task, and on the holder when it is in the same project. A park or a dead
session releases the hold.

[Relay identity](#relay-identity-opt-in) covers keying claims by harness session, PID
views, `unverifiable` claims, and `tasks release`.

<a id="session-selection"></a>

### Session envelope

`TASKS_MAX_COMPLEXITY` per harness process is the envelope a session picks within:
`ready`, `next`, and `prime` hide tasks rated above it and unassessed tasks, and say how
many. `--max-complexity` on `ready`/`next` overrides it for one call. Design:
`docs/specs/2026-09-12-task-complexity-design.md`.
`TASKS_WITHOUT` (comma-separated need names) is the other half of a session's envelope:
`ready`, `next`, and `prime` hide tasks needing any of them, in the projects that declare
the name, and say how many.
`--without` adds to it for one call and refuses a name no project in scope declares; the
variable never errors, so a host in ordinary use can set `TASKS_WITHOUT=quiet` once for
every project. Needs are declared per project in `[needs]` (see the design's §6). Design:
`docs/specs/2026-10-03-lanes-needs-groups-design.md`.

## Reference

### Command tour

    cd <repo>
    tasks init --prefix sci          # creates tasks/ and the doc roots; registers the project
    tasks init --prefix sci --force  # re-point the prefix here after moving the repo
    tasks unregister sci             # drop a stale prefix and its aliases; files are untouched
    tasks retire --successor mind6 --reason "superseded"  # declare this project over; unretire undoes it
    tasks rename dot dots            # rename a registered prefix; old ids still resolve
    tasks rename dot dots --explain  # diagnose an interruption without locks or writes
    tasks add "Bank the ledger" -p 1 --size m --complexity low --process direct --tag ledger --agent codex/gpt-6
    tasks add "Emit rows" --parent sci-4f2a9c
    tasks edit <id> --process planned # choose a workflow explicitly
    tasks edit <id> --no-process     # clear it to unassessed
    tasks add "Curation sweep" --every 30d  # days or weeks since each completion
    tasks list --periodic            # recurring tasks, soonest due first
    tasks edit <sweep-id> --every 2w # change the cadence; --no-every clears it and its anchor
    tasks add "Revisit the cache idea" --status idea --defer 60d  # hidden from the pickers until then
    tasks list --deferred            # deferred tasks, soonest first; due ones lead
    tasks edit <id> --no-defer       # clear it; any status change clears it too
    tasks add "Reply to Dana" --source "mail:<42@example.org>"  # where it came from; never interpreted
    tasks add "Reply to Dana" --source "mail:<42@example.org>"  # again: reuses the id, writes nothing
    tasks list --source "mail:<42@example.org>"  # what came from this reference (exact match)
    tasks list -p 0 -p 1 --size s --size xs   # P0 or P1, and small or extra-small
    tasks search "claim identity" --all-projects  # title or body contains the phrase; every list option applies
    tasks docs --kind plan --search "records root"  # working documents and the tasks linking them; also --all-projects
    tasks ready --complexity none             # ready work nobody has rated yet
    tasks ready                      # what can be worked on now (JSON)
    tasks ready --parallel -n 3      # up to 3 candidates marked safe to dispatch together
    tasks add "Capture lane" --lane -p 1 -b "Why it runs; first milestone"  # an effort beside the others
    tasks edit <id> --no-lane        # clear the lane marker
    tasks lanes                      # each lane: guidance, state, and the step it could take now
    tasks blockers                   # open prerequisites ranked by the open work they hold up
    tasks blockers --all-projects -n 0  # totals and coverage only, every reachable project
    tasks next --under sci-4f2a9c    # the next step inside one lane, at any depth
    tasks list --under sci-4f2a9c    # a goal's whole subtree (--parent is direct children)
    tasks block sci-4f2a9c "host busy"  # pause a lane; tasks unblock resumes it
    tasks add "Capture the trace" --need quiet  # a shared resource from [needs] in tasks/.config.toml
    tasks edit <id> --rm-need quiet  # --need adds; --rm-need/--no-needs remove
    tasks list --need quiet          # tasks that need it (all-of, like --tag)
    tasks ready --without quiet      # hide steps this session cannot meet; also TASKS_WITHOUT
    tasks sample --limit 3           # random open tasks for a curation pass (see skills/curate)
    tasks tree                       # the goal hierarchy
    tasks next                       # parked work waiting on you, else the first ready task
    tasks park <id> "next step" --reason review   # set it down; tasks list --parked to see what is parked
    tasks park <id> "rerun the preflight" --reason quiet --waiting-on user --minutes 50  # needs an idle host
    tasks quiet                      # what could run tonight, across every project; -n 1 for the top
    tasks list --parked --waiting-on user --all-projects  # everything waiting on you, with its next step
    tasks --pretty --headers list     # label each column of a pretty table
    tasks claims                     # every claim in every project's store; live = held (unverified: why it could not be judged here); what a Stop hook reads
    tasks release <id> "sandbox exited"  # drop a claim this command cannot judge, holder known gone; records why
    tasks release new-4f2a9c "gone" --adopting old  # the same for a claim recorded before a rename this host has not adopted
    tasks shelve <id> "when the dependency lands" # keep open work out of active views
    tasks unshelve <id>             # return shelved work to idea
    tasks next --all-projects        # the same across every registered project
    tasks prime --project fam        # read another registered project; also list, ready,
                                     #   next, tree, tags, sample, docs, blockers. Needs no local project.
    tasks projects                   # the registry: reachable? counts?
    tasks group set vf nodes atoms   # a named set of registered projects (this host only)
    tasks ready --group vf           # read a group; also list, next, prime, tree, tags,
                                     #   sample, lanes, quiet, docs, blockers. Needs no local project.
    tasks groups                     # each group, its members, and whether they are reachable
    tasks group rm vf                # delete the group; its projects stay registered
    tasks move dots-5760ef --to wali  # preserve the task, notes and attachments in another project
    tasks move dots-5760ef --to wali --explain  # diagnose without locks or writes
    tasks add "Piece" --project fam  # create in another registered project
    tasks note fam-0c3d7e "…"        # id-taking commands follow the prefix to its project
    tasks show 4f2a9c                # a bare suffix means the current project's task (sci-4f2a9c)
    tasks edit sci-4f2a9c --tag cli --rm-tag triage  # --tag adds; --rm-tag/--no-tags remove
    tasks edit sci-4f2a9c --depends sci-7b1e04       # --depends adds; --no-depends clears
    tasks dep sci-4f2a9c --on sci-7b1e04 --rm sci-0c3d7e  # swap a dependency in one save
    tasks --pretty ready             # same, as a table (or export TASKS_FORMAT=pretty)
    tasks --pretty --color auto ready # color when stdout is a terminal
    tasks start sci-4f2a9c
    tasks start sci-4f2a9c --force --reason "restore the service"  # audited halt or held-need override
    tasks note sci-4f2a9c "spec §4 no longer holds"
    tasks attach sci-4f2a9c ~/Pictures/before.png --caption "the stale row"  # copy into tasks/files/<id>/
    tasks attach sci-4f2a9c --clipboard       # an image from wl-paste; --name to choose the name
    tasks detach sci-4f2a9c before.png "wrong screenshot"  # recorded; uncommitted bytes are gone
    tasks done sci-91be03 "rows emitted"
    tasks done sci-4f2a9c "landed in 1a2b3c"  # open-work rule: closes once its child is closed
    tasks check                      # validate files, links, plan steps, dependencies; silent when clean
    tasks commit [--project <p>]     # commit every uncommitted file under tasks/, ignoring [git] commit

Run `tasks --help` for the full command list.

`tasks edit <id>` without field flags opens `$EDITOR` when stdin is a terminal.
Without a terminal it refuses before creating an edit copy or running the editor;
pass field flags (`tasks edit --help`) for automation. Use `tasks edit <id> --editor`
to explicitly run a scripted or GUI editor even without a terminal. `--editor`
cannot be combined with field flags.

### Output and errors

`tasks --help` lists every command and `tasks help <command>` one command's; add
`--pretty` to any command, before or after its name, for human-readable output (`--json`
is the default, spelled out). A usage error — an unknown command or option, a missing
argument, a value outside a closed set — exits 2 with the problem and the usage line on
stderr; a command that ran and failed exits 1 with one JSON error object there.

JSON task records omit unset optional fields and empty task collections (`tags`,
`depends`, `notes`, `refs`, `depends_on`, `children`). Missing means unset or empty; consumers
must not require those keys. Values such as `false`, `0`, and `body: ""` remain.
Response containers such as `tasks: []` and `warnings: []` remain, as does `next: null`
when nothing is eligible. See
[the output contract](docs/specs/2026-08-29-tasks-design.md#51-output-contract).

`check` warnings distinguish `doc_unreachable` (this host could not resolve a
reference) from `doc_unchecked` (one summary listing external checks unfinished
because the shared fetch budget ended). Warning-only checks exit 0; a warning
does not verify a document. Finding consumers, including obs and the TUI, must
recognize both kinds. Summary and parked rows include `step` only when set.
`tasks doc` exports exact UTF-8 body bytes in every format, with warnings on
stderr and no JSON envelope.

Task ids on the command line accept trailing sentence punctuation: a trailing run of
ASCII periods and commas on any positional id or id-valued flag (`--parent`, `--depends`,
`dep --on/--rm`, `feedback --recur`) is stripped before validation and alias resolution,
so an id copied from a sentence or a list works. Embedded or leading punctuation, other
punctuation, and leading or trailing whitespace are not accepted; records on disk and
every output stay canonical.

<a id="project-routing"></a>

### Routing across projects

Commands targeting an existing id, including `show`, `tree <id>`, `note`, and `start`,
work from outside every project: the prefix selects the registered root. Inside a
project, a matching prefix keeps the current checkout, including a worktree selected
with `-C`. `feedback` works there too and reports as `from:unregistered`.

ID-valued read filters follow the same routing: `--parent` and `--under` on
`list`, `search` and `ready`, and `next --under`, select the ID's project both
inside and outside another project. A matching prefix keeps the current checkout
or worktree. With both filters, their canonical prefixes must agree; retired
spellings and trailing sentence punctuation are accepted as on positional IDs.
A bare suffix always names the original cwd's project, including with `-C`;
routing or an explicit scope never changes that meaning.

An explicit `--project`, `--group` or `--all-projects` takes precedence. Filters
then narrow that scope: a target outside it is `task_not_found`. A parent and
ancestor in different projects have an empty intersection even in a wide scope.
`--source`, `--plan` and `--ref` remain literal filters and never select a project.
For provenance searches from outside every project, set the scope explicitly:

    tasks list --all-projects --source ops-2fe949 --status todo

Without a scope or an ID filter, these reads report `no_project` and suggest
`--all-projects` or `--project <prefix>`. Broken local metadata still fails rather
than being bypassed for a foreign ID.

Completion for these ID filters and `tree <id>` follows a typed foreign prefix
such as `ops-`, while a matching prefix keeps local/worktree candidates. Explicit
scopes still limit candidates. An empty fragment offers local IDs only; outside
every project it neither enumerates the registry nor offers bare suffixes.

The registry can also declare project groups (`[groups]`), named sets of live prefixes
that `--group <name>` reads together. `rename` carries a member to its new prefix.
`unregister` removes the prefix from every group and deletes, with a warning, any group it
leaves empty. A group name is never a live or retired prefix.

<a id="agent-and-completion-stamps"></a>

### Creation and completion stamps

`TASKS_MODEL` per harness process records which model completed each task: a fresh
`done` stamps the record's `model` field from it (and clears the stamp when it is
unset); correct a wrong stamp with `tasks edit --model`/`--no-model`.
`TASKS_AGENT` per harness process records which harness and model filed each task
(`<harness>/<model>`, or the harness alone): `add` and `feedback` stamp the record's
`agent` field from it, `add --agent` overrides it, and `tasks edit --agent`/`--no-agent`
corrects a stamp. The harness owns exporting it: Claude Code is wired through the ops
`claude-provenance` hook (session start and model switch, so the stamp follows
`/model`), Codex exports the harness alone, and other harnesses pass `--agent` when
they know their ids. Design:
`docs/specs/2026-09-13-creation-provenance-design.md`.

<a id="lifecycle-provenance"></a>

### Lifecycle notes

Lifecycle notes automatically record native harness provenance, independently of
claim identity and liveness. A stamped note has one indented JSON continuation:

```markdown
- 2026-09-17T20:00:00Z (worker): started
  provenance: {"harness_session":"codex:example","harness_session_source":"CODEX_SESSION_ID"}
```

`tasks show` exposes these optional fields directly on the note; both are absent
when unknown. The source names only `CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID`, `CODEX_SESSION_ID`,
or `CODEX_THREAD_ID`, with a matching `claude-code:` or `codex:` key. Codex
selects `CODEX_THREAD_ID` whenever present, including equal root/thread IDs;
otherwise it selects `CODEX_SESSION_ID`. Unequal valid IDs name a worker and its
shared root, and produce worker provenance without changing the serialized pair.
Historical stamps retain their recorded source. Missing/empty native values leave both fields
absent; conflicting or invalid inputs also leave them absent and emit a warning,
without blocking an otherwise valid lifecycle operation. A qualified `TASKS_SESSION`
override that disagrees with the native key is a conflict; a matching override never
replaces the native source. Other claim overrides remain independent. Do not set
`TASKS_SESSION` merely to improve observability: it is a claim override, not a
provenance source. Claim identity reads the same Codex variables on its own: a Codex
claim validates both native values and selects the thread when present, carries
no pid, and lives by the four-hour TTL. Malformed selected Codex input refuses
claim writes with repair or exact held `TASKS_SESSION` recovery guidance. With
only `CODEX_SESSION_ID`, workers cannot be distinguished from their controller.

Codex claims expose optional `root_session` in `show`, `prime` and `claims` and
persist it in the claim store as `codex:<root>`. It names the tree root, never an
immediate parent, and grants no ownership or shared holds. Native Codex sets it
from validated `CODEX_SESSION_ID`; explicit overrides and other harnesses omit it.
A same-owner refresh without root data retains the recorded root; conflicting
known roots refuse before mutation, including same-owner `start --force`. Inspect
`tasks show` and the exports, restore incorrect exports, or intentionally release
with `park` before starting under the new root. Takeovers record the new owner's
root, including absence. Release removes the metadata; lifecycle notes and parks gain no
root field. Old claims still load, but older writers may discard this field when
rewriting a store; participating sessions need the updated binary for retention.

The generated lifecycle texts are the consumer contract (including status edits):

- `started` on first start; `resumed` on subsequent starts, including owner refresh.
- `parked (waiting on …): <next step>`, using the existing park reason vocabulary.
- `done` or `dropped` on a genuine close transition.
- `completed; next due <YYYY-MM-DD>` instead of `done` for a recurring completion.
- `created` as the first note of every task `add` or `feedback` creates (author `add` or
  `feedback`); see Creation notes below. `feedback` recurrences write
  `feedback from <prefix>: <summary>` (and `detail from <prefix>: <body>`).

These notes persist after claims and parks are released. Close-message notes are also
stamped, but user messages are **not lifecycle markers**. Consumers such as obs derive
transition kinds from generated texts, not simply from the presence of provenance.
There is no serialized marker kind: arbitrary user text can equal a generated text
(for example, a close message of `resumed`). Text matching alone cannot disambiguate
that collision; consumers must retain that uncertainty.
Plain `tasks note`, shelf notes and takeover commentary remain unstamped.
`tasks note <id> "<text>" --stamp` opts one note in: it carries the same pair under the
same rules (a missing source leaves it off; a conflict warns without values and the note
still lands), and changes nothing else about `note`. Its text is not interpreted, so a
stamped note is no more a lifecycle marker than a close message is; flow's gate notes
use it to name the session at each stage boundary.

#### Creation notes

`add` and `feedback` write one note, text `created`, when they create a task (author
`add` or `feedback`). Its `at` equals the record's `created`, and it carries the same
native pair as other stamped notes under the same rules. When the pair comes from
`CODEX_THREAD_ID` and a valid `CODEX_SESSION_ID` differs from it, the note also carries
`root_session` (`codex:<root>`), the Codex tree root. Identity never blocks creation:
conflicting or invalid variables warn, naming variables and never values, and leave the
note unstamped. `TASKS_SESSION` is never a source. An `add` that reuses an existing
task via `--source` writes nothing.

A `feedback` recurrence stamps its `feedback from <prefix>: <summary>` note the same
way (pair and `root_session`); the following `detail from <prefix>: <body>` note
carries the pair alone. Each occurrence note's `at` is its own time, so a task that
recurs holds one stamped occurrence note per filing. Note texts are unchanged.

`add` and `feedback` JSON output gains `at`: the `at` of the occurrence note the
command wrote (absent for a `reused` add, which writes nothing). `add --pretty` still
prints only the id, and `feedback --pretty` still prints `<action> <id>`. Existing
records are not backfilled. A reader identifies the creation note as the first note
whose text is `created` and whose `at` equals the record's `created`; user text
equal to `created` elsewhere does not qualify.

Binaries older than the provenance writer reject a stamped file outright, so every host
that reads synced task files needs a current `tasks`. The contract and its rollout are
recorded in `docs/plans/2026-09-17-lifecycle-provenance.md`.

### Origin: whose ask a task is

`origin` records whose ask the record holds. It classifies the record's asks, not the
filing: who ran the command, or whether the agent filed on its own, never changes it.
A report that relays only the user's words is `user` even when the agent filed it
unprompted; it is `mixed` only when the agent also added an ask of its own.

| Value   | Meaning |
|---------|---------|
| `user`  | Every ask in the record comes from the user's own prompt: they described it, asked for it to be filed, or the report relays their words. |
| `agent` | No ask in the record comes from a user prompt: an agent's observation, follow-up, feedback report, decomposition piece, plan step, dependency or scope filing. |
| `mixed` | The record holds both: at least one ask from the user's prompt and at least one distinct ask the agent added. |
| absent  | Unknown. |

The filer supplies it from evidence in its own session, with `--origin <user|agent|mixed>`
on `add` and `feedback`; when unsure it omits the flag. The tool never derives it from
`agent`, `parent`, `source`, tags, session presence or commit time. `--origin-session
<key>` (`claude-code:<id>` or `codex:<id>`) names the session where the ask was made when
that is not the filing session; it is recorded on that occurrence's note only, says where
to look, and is not a claim that the user asked. A bad key is refused before anything is
written.

It lives in two places. Each occurrence note (the creation note and each `feedback from`
note) records the origin and origin session supplied at that occurrence; these never
change. The frontmatter field `origin` is the record's current judgment: set at creation,
combined on recurrence, corrected with `edit`.

A feedback recurrence labelled X updates the field: unchanged when the field equals X or
X is absent, or when the field is `mixed`; `mixed` when the field and X are different
known values. When the field is absent and X is known, the field stays absent and the
command warns that the record's origin is unknown and the occurrence says X; the note
keeps X.

`tasks edit <id> --origin <value>` corrects the field and `--no-origin` withdraws it;
notes are never touched. A corrector adds a stamped note citing evidence
(`tasks note <id> "<evidence>" --stamp`).

**Reading rule.** Every consumer reads origin one way:

1. When the field is set, it is the record's origin. It supersedes every occurrence
   label, including the creation label.
2. When the field is absent, the origin is unknown, but the occurrence labels are
   partial evidence: a label `user` or `mixed` means the record carries some of the
   user's words; otherwise the origin stays unknown.

Example: a task created with `--origin user` is corrected with `edit --origin agent`.
The field says `agent` while the creation note still says `user`; rule 1 gives `agent`,
and no user words. After `edit --no-origin` the field is absent and rule 2 sees the
`user` label again.

`list`, `search` and `ready` take `--origin <user|agent|mixed|none>`, repeatable and
widening; `none` selects tasks whose field is absent. Task JSON gains `origin` (omitted
when unset) and notes gain `origin` and `origin_session`, all additive. Existing records
are not backfilled. Rollout: binaries older than this reject records carrying the new
keys, so install the new `tasks` on every host that reads synced records before records
filed by it sync.

### Relay identity (opt-in)

A host that runs the relay agent registry can key claims by the harness
session itself rather than by the terminal. It is off by default; turn it on in
`~/.config/tasks/config.toml` (or `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/tasks/config.toml`):

```toml
[identity]
relay = true
```

The file is host-local on purpose. Whether relay runs is a property of a machine, while the
per-project `tasks/.config.toml` syncs between hosts, so the switch does not belong there.

Turn it on only where relay's hooks actually publish its agent registry. Every `tasks` command
run under a harness is in scope once the switch is on, and without the registry every
claim acquisition there refuses. Relay records the handle of the process that is the
session, so headless, nested and background sessions (`claude -p`, `claude --bg`,
`codex exec`) each claim as themselves.

With it on, `tasks` walks its own process ancestry to the nearest harness process —
`claude`, `codex` or `opencode`, or a versioned Claude Code binary under claude/versions/,
which is how a background session runs; Claude Code's own daemon and pty host are not
sessions and are refused — and looks that process up in relay's agent registry, matching on
host, boot id, pid and process start time, and requiring the registry's harness to agree
with the process it found. On a match the claim is keyed by the relay agent id —
`<harness>:<sessionId>`, such as `codex:01J…` — and records that agent's process handle as
the claim's proof. Because the id belongs to the session rather than to the terminal, a
claim survives the command that made it and is recognized again by the same session later.

That proof is also what the session's own commands read back: the owner can `park` or
`done` a claim it already holds even when the registry has gone away, because ownership is
re-derived from what the claim itself recorded. Two limits follow from the same rule.
Parking *releases* the claim, so resuming a parked task is a fresh acquisition and needs
either the registry back or `TASKS_SESSION`. And from 0.2.0, a session nested inside
another harness session is a different session: its nearest boundary is its own harness
process, so it cannot act on the outer session's claims.

Codex hints validate both native exports and select `CODEX_THREAD_ID` when present,
otherwise `CODEX_SESSION_ID`. A matching Codex actor row records native root
association separately. Relay publishes a row per Codex worker (`scope: "worker"`,
naming its `root`) on its controller's process. Among the rows on one process, the hint
selects the caller's own, and a worker row is selected only by that worker's
`CODEX_THREAD_ID`. A worker relay has not registered is refused rather than given its
controller's identity; other mismatches use a value-free diagnosis.

Codex proof-only continuation now requires a valid concrete `CODEX_THREAD_ID`
matching the held claim, plus the existing process, host and boot evidence.
A sibling, absent thread, session-only export, or malformed native value cannot
prove ownership. This deliberately removes the former thread-less process-proof
fallback. Exact resolved identity matches still work. A legitimate owner blocked
by missing thread data can inspect `tasks show <id>` and set `TASKS_SESSION` to
that exact held session; set `TASKS_SESSION_PID` only for an actual long-lived
process, never the command PID. Parentage and root association do not authorize
foreign claims. Normal workers release with `done` or `park --waiting-on agent`
before reporting completion; controllers run `start` before review or closure.
Agent-waiting parks are public to all agents. A controller uses forced takeover
only after a worker-specific completion result establishes that worker and its
checks have stopped; silence, a timeout and the shared PID do not establish it.

Relay process matching also requires hooks and task commands to share a PID
namespace. A sandbox exposing the Codex ancestor as PID 1 cannot match relay's
published host PID; this refuses acquisition, and no process evidence inside such a
sandbox can prove the session (tasks-fe6c59). The refusal names the PID namespace when
the nearest harness process is pid 1 with no parent, and recommends setting
`TASKS_SESSION` to the exact session without `TASKS_SESSION_PID` (a pid from inside the
namespace keeps the claim held after the session ends; see below), or running with the
host PID view. The live acceptance capture used a separately approved host-PID
invocation.

A claim records the PID view its pid was established in: the PID namespace that the
writer's `/proc` numbers pids in. Only a command in that same view judges the pid.
Elsewhere, and wherever either view is unknown, the claim is `unverifiable`: it is held,
and nothing prunes it, takes it over without `--force`, or releases its holds. A
reboot, its owner's `park` or `done`, or `start --force` clears it, and so does
`tasks release <id> "<why>"` once you know the holder is gone: it records why in one note
and leaves the task's lifecycle alone. An exported pid
(`TASKS_SESSION_PID`, `CLAUDE_PID`) establishes a view only in the initial PID
namespace, because an inherited number's namespace cannot be proven. Inside a container
or sandbox, such claims stay held after their session ends. `TASKS_SESSION_PID` must
name a process in the namespace of the command that sets it. A pid the command's own
`/proc` shows is not running (pid 0, a gone or zombie session leader, or an exported pid
gone or a zombie in the initial namespace) is not recorded: the claim lives by the TTL instead. In
a PID namespace whose session leader is outside it, the Unix session id reads 0 for
every shell, so the fallback refuses it; set `TASKS_SESSION` there.

**Upgrading.** tasks 0.2.0 reads relay's registry schema 2 and no other; against an older
registry it refuses and asks you to run `relay reap`. On a host with this switch on, every
`tasks` that can run there must be 0.2.0 or later before relay publishes schema 2: check
`tasks --version` for each `tasks` on `PATH` in each harness's environment. An older `tasks`
refuses fresh claims against the new registry, but it can still let a session nested inside
another continue the outer session's claims, which no registry format can prevent.

tasks 0.3.0 judges claims by PID view. Its protection holds only when every `tasks`
that reads or writes a host's claim stores is 0.3.0 or later: each `tasks` on `PATH`
in each harness's environment, including one a sandbox can execute. An older binary
judges every pid through its own `/proc`. It can prune a claim that another view holds,
it drops the recorded view when it saves, and it reports that claim as stale. Check
`tasks --version` for each.

Enabling relay never rewrites a claim already held: a claim keeps the identity it was
created with. The level is Linux-only — it needs `/proc` — and it sits *below*
`TASKS_SESSION` in the ladder, so an explicit `TASKS_SESSION` recovers from every relay
identity error and distinguishes agents sharing a process when native thread identity is
unavailable. Each error names the override to set: `TASKS_SESSION` and
`TASKS_SESSION_PID`, except the PID-namespace refusal above, which asks for
`TASKS_SESSION` alone. The override never supplies native note provenance.

### Choosing a process

Set `--process direct|planned` on `add` or `edit`; `edit --no-process` clears it.
Choose it alongside size and complexity when scoping work, including each plan child.
It is never derived from those fields, parentage, or document links. The
[Process](#process) concept tabulates what each value asks of an agent.

Both code paths retain appropriate debugging, tests, and review, and use an isolated
task worktree under the adopted policy. A direct task that uncovers an unresolved
design decision or grows beyond its scope needs a note and reassessment to planned.
Ideas still need scoping. Existing document links do not establish approval.

JSON task, summary, and parked rows expose `process` as a string when assessed;
unassessed rows omit it. Pretty summary and parked rows show a process column (`-` when unassessed); show and next
print a `process:` row reading `direct`, `planned`, or `unassessed`. The parked
`phase` remains a link-derived resume hint: a todo without document links can show
`phase: implementing` alongside `process: planned`, which still requires both reviews.

`tasks check` warns `process_missing` only for doing records without a choice,
including goals and plan steps. Unassessed todos need no backfill sweep. The CLI
does not change readiness, ordering, or `start` eligibility based on process, and
does not run skills or create worktrees.

Projects must adopt the process policy in their agent instructions (see the
[adoption snippet](#3-tell-the-projects-agents) under Setup) before it can take
precedence over generic brainstorming triggers.
This repo has adopted it. The writing-plans integration is the tasks skill's child
command (`--complexity <level> --process <value>`), not the upstream plan-writing skill.
Design: `docs/specs/2026-09-13-task-process-design.md`.

### Attachments

Attachments live in `tasks/files/<id>/`, one directory per task, committed with the
record. Each file is capped at 2 MiB unless `tasks/.config.toml` sets
`[attachments] max_bytes`. A task's own `attached: <name> (<n> bytes)` and
`detached: <name>: <why>` notes are the ledger of which files it owns. `show` lists
the files with absolute paths. `check` reports these kinds:

- errors: `attachment_unsafe`, `attachment_orphan`, `attachment_unnoted`, and
  `attachment_missing`;
- warnings: `attachment_invalid` and `attachment_too_large`.

`tasks/files/<id>` and its parent must be real directories, not symlinks.
Binaries older than attachments ignore tasks/files/ entirely. `feedback` never
carries attachments.

An interrupted `attach` leaves a file that `check` reports as `attachment_unnoted`.
Rerun it with the same bytes and `--name <name>` to finish, or `detach` the file. An
interrupted `detach` finishes when rerun.

### Moving tasks

`tasks move <id> --to <prefix> [--explain]` moves an open, unparented,
childless, unclaimed task from its registered checkout to another live registered
project. Destination validation still applies to its spec, plan, needs and dependencies.
It preserves fields, notes and live attachments, carries this host's park and escalation,
and leaves a read-only `moved` tombstone. Writes and new references to the tombstone
refuse with `moved`, naming the destination id. Existing dependents follow the pointer;
`check` warns `moved_dep` with `tasks dep <id> --on <new> --rm <old>` for their owners.
`show` displays the tombstone; `resolve` continues to resolve prefixes and paths only.

Task objects expose optional `moved_to` (the destination id on a source tombstone)
and `moved_from` (the source id on the destination). `status` includes `moved`, a
closed, read-only status; counts include `moved`, and `total` counts every record.
Only `move` sets the pointer fields. Older binaries cannot parse these records:
update every host reading synced tasks before the first move.

The move output (`MoveOut`) names the paths written in each root. Under `[git] commit`
it commits each opted-in root; otherwise commit each root its `paths` lists:

```json
{"id": "wali-b0882b", "from": "dots-5760ef", "recovery": "fresh",
 "attachments": ["shot.png"], "park": true, "inbound": ["ops-1a2b3c"],
 "paths": {"<dots root>": ["tasks/dots-5760ef.md", "tasks/files/dots-5760ef/shot.png"],
           "<wali root>": ["tasks/wali-b0882b.md", "tasks/files/wali-b0882b/shot.png"]},
 "warnings": []}
```

`recovery` is `fresh`, `resumed`, or `complete`; a rerun after success writes nothing.
`--explain` returns the same shape without locks or writes, including `refuse` with
reasons in `warnings`. For an interrupted move, `--explain` reports `resume`;
performing the recovery reports `resumed`. `id` is empty when refusal happens before
an id is minted.
`inbound` reports dependents found in reachable live registered projects; it cannot
inventory unreachable or retired projects. Rerun the same command after process interruption. A host-local
journal freezes writes to both ids and both projects' lifecycle commands with
`move_pending`. Reads remain available. `check` reports `move_pending` for a local
journal, `move_incomplete` for a reachable missing or mismatched counterpart, and
`move_counterpart_unreachable` when it cannot inspect the counterpart.
Recovery covers process interruption, not power loss; parks on other hosts stay keyed
to the old id. See [recovery limits and manual undo](docs/specs/2026-10-08-task-move-design.md#44-recovery-limits).

### Task references

Alongside the governing `--spec` and `--plan` links, `add --ref` and `edit --ref`
accept repeatable reference entries. The binary stores them in a managed
`## References` section between the body and `## Notes`; do not put that heading
in `--body`. Each stored line uses this grammar (omit the leading `- ` in `--ref`):

```text
- <handle> (<relation>[, required][, kind=<kind>]): <reference>[ — <description>]
```

Handles match `[a-z][a-z0-9-]{0,31}` and are unique within the task. Relations are
`context` (consult when needed), `input` (used by the work), or `output` (produced
or revised by the work). `required` marks an entry for reading before work;
`kind` is a descriptive label matching `[a-z][a-z0-9-]*`. Attributes stay in the
order shown. Descriptions follow a space, em dash, and space.

A reference is a normalized repo-relative file or directory path (no trailing
slash), an attachment `files:<name>`, or an external `<scheme>:<remainder>`.
Cross-project `@` references are not supported. References containing whitespace,
`"`, or `\` must be double-quoted, with `\"` and `\\` as the only escapes.
Decoded references must also be unique within a task. New or changed context
and input targets must exist locally or be attached; outputs may be pending.
External entries are validated for shape without fetching.

```sh
tasks add "Revise the runbook" \
  --ref 'brief (input, required, kind=brief): docs/notes/brief.md — admission rules' \
  --ref 'runbook (output, required, kind=runbook): "docs/runbooks/trigger sweep.md"' \
  --body 'Follow [ref:brief] §7 and revise [ref:runbook].'
tasks edit <id> --ref 'brief (input, required): docs/notes/revised-brief.md'
tasks edit <id> --rm-ref brief --body 'Revise [ref:runbook].'
tasks edit <id> --no-refs --body 'References no longer needed.'
```

`edit --ref` replaces an existing handle in place or appends a new one.
`--rm-ref` is repeatable; `--no-refs` clears all entries and conflicts with
`--ref` and `--rm-ref`. A body citation is `[ref:<handle>]`; unknown or malformed
handles are refused when saving body or entry changes, and reported by `check`
for open tasks. Citation syntax inside CommonMark code spans or fenced or
indented code blocks is literal. Notes are not audited. Remove citations when
removing their entries, replacing the body in the same call if needed.

```sh
tasks doc <id> brief            # exact UTF-8 text, without an envelope
tasks list --ref docs/notes/brief.md
tasks search "runbook" --ref docs/notes/brief.md
```

`doc` accepts exactly one handle, `--spec`, or `--plan`. Directories and binary
files fail as `ref_not_text`; pending outputs fail as `doc_not_found`. External
entries use the host's document provider and respect `--no-fetch`.
`list --ref` and `search --ref` match the stored reference byte for byte,
without fetching or alias resolution.

`show` includes an optional `inventory`: spec, plan, explicit entries in order,
source, then unreferenced attached files in name order. Rows report origin,
location, status and any entry metadata. Entries matching a spec or plan merge
into its row when both resolve to the same target; an attachment entry replaces
its standalone attachment row. Required rows form the reading list in inventory
order: spec and plan are always required, then entries marked `required`.
Missing outputs show as `pending`; external entries are not fetched for inventory.
Full task objects expose `refs` only when nonempty; summary rows omit it.

Every fresh transition to `done`, including `edit --status done` and the editor,
requires local output paths and output attachments to exist (`ref_output_missing`).
Produce them or explicitly remove their entries; `--force` does not bypass this
gate. Special files are refused. External outputs and `drop` are not checked.
Each reopened or recurring completion is checked; repeating `done` on an already
completed task still releases its claim even if an output has since disappeared.

Closed records (`done`, `dropped`, and `moved`) keep their historical plan and step
links. If the plan is absent from both the record's checkout and its main checkout,
`show` returns the record with a warning that the plan is unavailable and
`step_found: false` when a step is linked. Available plans still have their steps
checked; missing local plans for open work and other local read errors still fail.
External availability follows the contract below.

### Working documents

`tasks docs` lists a project's working documents with the tasks that link them, so a
document moved out of the code tree stays findable:

```sh
tasks docs                                   # every working document of this project
tasks docs --kind plan --kind spec           # repeats widen: spec, plan, brief, handoff, note
tasks docs --all-projects --search "records root"  # title or body, matched as search matches
```

The working documents are the Markdown files directly under the project's spec and
plan directories (`spec_dirs` and `plan_dirs`, which default to `docs/specs`,
`docs/plans` and the older design-document locations) and `docs/notes`, read from its
`records` directory. Their kind comes
from the directory, then the filename (`*-brief.md`, `*-handoff.md`, else `note`); a
detached project's reference documents in its code tree are not listed. Each row has
`project`, `kind`, `path` (as a task stores the link), `file` (absolute), `title` (the
first level-one heading, else the file's stem) and `tasks`: every task, of any status,
whose `spec`, `plan` or a `--ref` entry stores exactly that path, as
`{"id","status","via"}` with `via` one of `spec`, `plan` or `ref`, plus `handle` for a
reference. A file that is not UTF-8 is listed under its stem with a warning and never
matches `--search`; a `.md` symlink to nothing is a warning, and an unreadable file
fails the command with an `io` error naming it. `tasks doc <id> --spec|--plan|<handle>` reads one.

### External documents

`--spec` and `--plan` also accept `<scheme>:<remainder>`, for example
`mindful:thought:abc`. The scheme matches `[a-z][a-z0-9-]*`; the nonempty
remainder is opaque and may contain further colons, slashes, spaces and quotes,
but no newline, carriage return or NUL. A colon in the first path segment
reserves the external form; `docs/plans/x:y.md` remains local. Configured
`spec_dirs` and `plan_dirs` cannot contain a colon in their first segment.

Configure fetch commands on each host in `~/.config/tasks/config.toml`:

```toml
[docs.schemes]
mindful = "mindful-doc"
```

The command is trusted host configuration. Tasks invokes
`sh -c '<command> "$1"' -- <remainder>` with closed stdin, so the reference is
one literal argument. The command must return one UTF-8 JSON object with string
`id` and `body` fields; `id` is nonempty and single-line, without NUL. Extra
fields are allowed. Tasks stores `<scheme>:<id>` after a successful write.
Each fetch has a 30-second deadline, a 2 MiB stdout limit and a diagnostic
prefix of at most 200 stderr bytes. Remaining processes in its group are
terminated when the shell exits or a limit is reached. Providers must keep
children in that group and must not daemonize; escaped jobs are their
responsibility. Pipe reads remain deadline-bounded even if a provider violates
that restriction.

Writes fetch only changed external links and verify an external step only when
its plan or step changed. Unrelated title, priority or body edits work without
the scheme. Changing an alias counts as a change. Adding links, exporting a
document and moving a task with an external step require successful reads.
A move without a step preserves external references without fetching.

`check` uses up to four concurrent fetches within one five-second budget. It
prioritizes open plans with steps, other open plans, open specs, then closed-only
plans; within each tier references sort lexically. A shared reference belongs
to its highest tier and is read once. Missing schemes or attempted provider
failures produce per-task `doc_unreachable` warnings for open work. Budget
exhaustion produces one `doc_unchecked` summary listing unfinished references
in priority order. Local checks continue; available plans still produce errors
for missing steps. Malformed host configuration remains fatal.

`show` and `next` spend at most five seconds fetching a stepped external plan.
An unavailable open plan gives a warning and omits `step_found`; a closed task
uses `step_found: false` with a historical warning. Without a step they do not
fetch the external plan, and spec links do not trigger fetches. Displayed
`spec_path` and `plan_path` are the stored external references; local links
remain absolute paths.

`show --no-fetch`, `next --no-fetch` and `doc --no-fetch` never run a provider
command, for a caller that must stay read-only on a host with `[docs.schemes]`.
`show` and `next` then omit `step_found` for an external plan, open or closed,
without a warning: a skipped fetch says nothing about availability. `doc` fails
an external link as `doc_not_found` (`fetch disabled by --no-fetch`). Local
documents read as usual.

```sh
tasks doc <id> --plan       # exactly one of --plan, --spec, or a reference handle
tasks doc <id> --spec
tasks list --plan mindful:thought:abc --status done
tasks search "phrase" --plan mindful:thought:abc
```

`doc` returns only the selected document's exact body, even with `--json` or
`--pretty`, and adds no newline, color or headers. `--plan` on list/search is
an exact comparison against the stored reference: no fetch, alias resolution
or parent restriction. Local paths use the same exact comparison. Optional
`step` is exposed in JSON rows without adding a pretty table column.

Upgrade each host's binary before adding `[docs.schemes]` on that host: older
binaries reject the table. Upgrade every host reading synced records before
the first external link. Roll back by removing the table before restoring an
older binary, and remove external links before reverting every reader.
The workflow activation pilot must show three clean full-backlog checks on
each host with its real wrapper and web app running, under five seconds with
no `doc_unchecked`. Failed pilots require a faster provider before activation;
later `doc_unchecked` findings are latency incidents. Provider rollout and pilot
evidence belong to the ops rollout task, `ops-721511`.

<a id="prefix-renames-and-recovery"></a>

### Renaming a prefix

The registry maps live prefixes to project roots and retired prefixes to their current
live name. `tasks rename <old> <new>` updates the project's filenames, ids, local
`depends`/`parent` references, config, and registry. References in other projects and in
prose need no edits: retired names keep resolving **for as long as the project stays
registered**. `unregister` removes that project's aliases too; retired names cannot be
reused while registered.

A live id and its retired spelling are one task. `tasks dep <id> --on <x>` when the task
already depends on `x` under any spelling changes nothing, keeps the stored spelling, and
says so in `warnings`; `--rm` with either spelling removes that one dependency. An
`--on`/`--rm` pair therefore cannot rewrite a stored retired prefix: in two calls it drops
the edge, and in one call it is refused because both flags name the same task.

Rename requires clean `tasks/`, no live claims, and at most one git worktree. An interrupted
rename freezes writes to that project; reads remain available. Re-run the same command to
resume, or use `--explain` to observe its recovery verdict without writing, locking, or
checking authorization. Outside git, rename warns that forward recovery is the only
option after source removal. `git checkout .` alone does not undo a rename; see
[manual recovery](docs/specs/2026-09-08-prefix-rename-design.md#56-undo-and-manual-recovery).

Attachment directories move with their records. The inventory records which tasks had
attachments, and recovery refuses R9 (unexpected destination attachments), R10
(attachments missing from both sides), or R11 (source attachments appeared after the
inventory).

An inventory written by a binary older than attachments fails to load, and since every
mutating command checks the host's pending renames, that blocks mutating commands in
every project on the host, not only the one being renamed. Finish that rename with the
older binary, then `git mv tasks/files/<old>-<hex> tasks/files/<new>-<hex>` for each
task directory.

If another host already renamed a synced checkout, run `tasks rename <old> <new> --adopt`
from that checkout on this host **before starting work there**. It changes only this host's
registry and claim state; old ids keep resolving. A live old or new claim blocks adoption:
stop its owning session or wait for it to become stale, then retry. For a rehearsal, set
both `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` and `XDG_STATE_HOME` to scratch directories so no live registry or
park is touched. `--explain --adopt` diagnoses the local state without writes.

#### Location history

The host-local registry's optional `[locations.<prefix>]` table records the current
root's symlinked worktree `storage` and `former` roots, each with optional storage and
a UTC `until` date. Paths must be absolute; history is not synced between hosts.

| Command | Location history |
| --- | --- |
| `init` | Records current storage. |
| `init --prefix <p> --force` at the same root | Refreshes current storage. |
| `init --prefix <p> --force` at a new root | Records the former root and storage, then refreshes current storage. |
| `rename <old> <new>` | Carries history to the new prefix and refreshes storage. |
| `rename <old> <new> --adopt` | Merges both prefixes' history, records a displaced root, and refreshes storage. |
| `unregister <p>` | Removes that project's history. |

Before moving a checkout, run `tasks -C <root> init --prefix <p> --force` on every
other host while the old root and storage still exist. Without that record, adoption
can retain the former root but may lack its storage and warn. A dangling link at an
unchanged root preserves recorded storage; after a root change it clears the current
storage record. Former entries remain until unregistering.

For a move made before location history was available, backfill the former root in
that host's `~/.config/tasks/projects.toml`, substituting its absolute paths:

```toml
[locations.tack]
former = [
  { root = "<Dropbox>/ai", storage = "<WORK_ROOT>/ai/.worktrees", until = "2026-09-27" },
]
```

Preserve existing history when adding an entry, then run
`tasks -C <root> init --prefix tack --force` to refresh current storage. An older
`tasks` binary drops `[locations]` whenever it writes the registry; update each host's
binary before recording history.

### Retiring a project

A project that is over declares it in its own `tasks/.config.toml` with `tasks retire
[--successor <prefix>] --reason "<one line>"`, run in its registered checkout. It refuses
while any task is open in any checkout, while a claim is live, or while a linked worktree
cannot be read, and writes a `[retired]` table (`date`, `reason`, optional `successor`,
stored as the successor's live prefix). It refuses an already retired project too:
`tasks unretire` first to declare it again. From then on every write to the project is
refused with `retired_project`, from every checkout, a worktree made before the
retirement included, whose `tasks check` also reports its open work; its ids keep
resolving and satisfy other projects' dependencies; `--all-projects` and `--group` reads
and their id completion leave it out, as does the list of feedback owners, while
`--project` reads and `show` warn; `tasks projects` keeps its row with `retired`;
`group set` refuses it as a member; `init --force` and `rename` refuse it. `tasks
unretire` in the registered checkout removes the table. The project lifecycle runbook in
ops has the whole procedure.

### Linked and detached projects

A linked project keeps its task records, specs, and plans in an overlay project directory
while its code lives in another git checkout. Run this in the overlay project directory:

    tasks init --prefix <p> --checkout <path>

Its `tasks/.config.toml` carries `[checkout] path`, written relative to the project root
(absolute paths are accepted when read). Commands run in the code checkout or its
worktrees open the linked project; nothing is written into the code tree. Claims and
parks name the code worktree, so resume there. `tasks projects --json` rows carry
an absolute `checkout`; `check` warns `checkout_missing` when the
checkout is absent on this host. `resolve` matches it with `via: "checkout"`, and the
storage its `.worktrees` link points into, removed worktrees included, with `via: "storage"`,
while that link stands; nothing records it.

`tasks where [PATH] --json` reports which project a directory or file opens. In git,
it stays within that repository; outside git it walks up to find a project. Its three
outcomes are:

- Project found: `{"project":{"prefix":"<p>","root":"<overlay>","checkout":"<code>","records":"<overlay>","kind":"linked","linked":true},"holds_records":false,"warnings":[]}`.
  Every project reports `kind` (`in-tree`, `detached` or `linked`), `records` and
  `checkout` as strings; an in-tree project has all three paths equal to `root`, with
  `linked: false`. `linked` equals `kind == "linked"`. `color` is present when the
  project sets one.
- No project: `{"project":null,"holds_records":false,"warnings":[]}`.
- Error: exit 1 with `{"error":{"kind":"<kind>","detail":"<detail>"}}` on stderr;
  success JSON is on stdout with exit 0.

`holds_records` reports whether the repository keeps a project's records. It is true
when an existing registered root lies in one of the repository's worktrees and shares
its common git directory, so a registered project counts even on an unborn branch. It
is also true when the repository tracks a regular `tasks/.config.toml` file in `HEAD`,
even if that file is deleted locally. An unborn branch with no registered root holds
none. Two
projects declaring the same checkout fail with `checkout_conflict`. Init refuses
writes into a declared code checkout or any of its worktrees.

#### Detached projects

A detached project keeps its records and working documents in a separate records
repository, at `<records-root>/<prefix>`, while the code checkout stays free of them.
Every project has three locations:

| field | meaning | in-tree | detached | linked |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `root` | the registered root; what `tasks root` prints | the checkout | the checkout | `<overlay>/<prefix>` |
| `checkout` | the code checkout sessions run in | = root | = root | the foreign repository |
| `records` | where `tasks/` and `docs/` live | = root | `<records-root>/<prefix>` | = root |

Run this in the code checkout:

    tasks init --prefix <p> --records <records-root>

It writes `<records-root>/<p>/tasks/.config.toml` with the prefix, `[git] commit = true`,
`[checkout] path` (relative to the records directory, for example `../../<code>`) and
`[checkout] kind = "detached"`, creates `docs/specs` and `docs/plans` there, and pairs
the registry. Nothing is written in the checkout. On an existing records config (a
migration) it keeps the file and its comments, adds `[checkout]`, and sets
`[git] commit = true` when absent or false; a prefix mismatch is a `config` error. The
second host runs the same command after the records sync, and only its registry is
written. `--records` excludes `--checkout`. `--force` repoints as before and keeps
aliases, groups and location history.

The registry gains a `[records]` table beside `[projects]`:

```toml
[projects]
tack = "<code>"

[records]
tack = "<records-root>/tack"
```

Init refuses with:

- `records_in_tree`: `tasks/.config.toml` is still in the checkout's working tree or
  index. Remove it with `git rm -r tasks`. A HEAD that still tracks it while the index
  deletes it is allowed, so the removal commit's `tasks check` passes.
- `checkout_conflict`: another prefix declares this checkout.
- `config`: the checkout overlaps another registered project (containment either way
  or a shared git common directory), is a linked worktree rather than a main checkout,
  or the records root does not exist; or, without `--force`, the prefix is already
  paired with another records directory (with `--force` the pairing is replaced and a
  warning names the old one).
- `retired_project`: the existing records config declares `[retired]` and `--force`
  was used.

A plain `init` that registers or repoints a prefix to an in-tree or linked root drops its
`[records]` pairing with a warning; a plain `init` in a checkout paired in `[records]`
refuses with `records_moved`, and one in a detached records directory refuses with
`config`, naming the `init --records` to run from its checkout. A registry that maps a
prefix to a detached records directory without a `[records]` row is a `config` error
for every command that opens it.

Commands run in the code checkout or any of its worktrees open the detached project
through the registry pairing; `-C <records-root>/<p>` opens it by the config walk.
Documents (`--spec`, `--plan`, `--ref`, `--source` paths) resolve under `records`
first, then the code worktree the command runs in, then the code main checkout, so a
reference document kept in the code tree still links and `check` does not warn
`ref_in_main_checkout` for it. `check` warns `checkout_missing` when the code checkout
is absent on this host, for detached and linked projects alike.

Git queries and record commits select their repository by path, ignoring inherited
`GIT_DIR`, `GIT_COMMON_DIR`, `GIT_WORK_TREE` and `GIT_INDEX_FILE` from a calling hook.
The migration guard's code-index check keeps the hook's index, so a staged removal
is judged against the index being committed.

A detached project in `tasks where --json`:

    {"project":{"prefix":"<p>","root":"<code>","checkout":"<code>","records":"<records-root>/<p>","kind":"detached","linked":false},"holds_records":false,"warnings":[]}

Pretty `where` prints `<p> <root> (records at <records>)`. In the detached code
checkout `holds_records` is false unless HEAD still tracks the config; inside the
records repository it is true. `tasks projects` rows carry `records` always, and
`checkout` and `kind` whenever the config was read; an unreachable row has `records`
(from the pairing or the root) but neither `checkout` nor `kind`. `projects --paths`
appends ` → <records>` on a detached row, and `resolve` rows gain `records`, with
`via: "records"` for a path under a records directory.

`where` outside git reads no registry, so a copied historical config outside git opens
there while `locate` refuses it.

Two errors guard against the split:

- `records_moved`: a `tasks/.config.toml` found in a code tree (an old branch) whose
  prefix is paired elsewhere, from every command and from `check` when the index still
  holds the file. The detail names the records directory. Rebase or merge the branch
  onto the main branch; that tree's `tasks/` is read-only history.
- `records_unpaired`: a registered root with no config and no `[records]` row, as on a
  second host before its own `init --records`, from its checkout and from every command
  that names the prefix (`--project`, an id, `move --to`). The detail names `init
  --prefix <p> --records <records-root>` first, then plain `init` for a root that keeps
  no records anywhere.

A malformed registry is a `config` error for every command.

`rename <old> <new>` on a detached project moves `<records-root>/<old>` to
`<records-root>/<new>` as one resumable stage (`records` in `TASKS_RENAME_STOP_AFTER`),
updates the `[records]` key and value in the same registry save, and leaves `[checkout]
path` unchanged. It leaves the directory rename uncommitted: commit it in the records
repository. The usual refusals apply against the records repository (clean `tasks/`, no
live claims, at most one worktree). On the second host, `rename --adopt` pairs the
renamed directory; a plain `rename` there, finding the old directory gone and the new
one present with no rename in progress, refuses with `validation` naming `--adopt`.

Update each host's binary before the first detached project. An older binary cannot
parse `kind = "detached"`, and it drops the `[records]` table on its next registry
save.

### Resolving ids and paths

Use `tasks resolve <id|prefix|path>...` or `tasks resolve --stdin` (one input per line)
to map inputs through prefix renames and directory moves. It is read-only and needs no
current project. Paths containing `/` or beginning with `.` or `~` are classified
first, then full ids, then prefixes matching `[a-z][a-z0-9]{1,7}`, then invalid inputs.
Relative paths use the working directory, or `-C` if supplied. Bare hex shorthand is
not expanded: `beef00` is a prefix, while `4f2a9c` is invalid. Id resolution does not
check whether the task file exists; use `tasks show` for that.

```json
{"results": [
  {"input": "ai-1a2b3c", "kind": "id", "status": "resolved",
   "id": "hq-1a2b3c", "prefix": "hq", "alias": "ai", "root": "<Dropbox>/hq"},
  {"input": "zz-123456", "kind": "id", "status": "unregistered", "prefix": "zz"},
  {"input": "/x/y", "kind": "path", "status": "ambiguous",
   "candidates": [{"prefix": "aa", "via": "former_root", "location": "/x"},
                  {"prefix": "bb", "via": "former_root", "location": "/x"}]},
  {"input": "4f2a9c", "kind": "invalid", "status": "invalid",
   "detail": "expected an id <prefix>-<hex6>, a prefix, or a path"}
], "warnings": []}
```

Resolved paths include `via` and `location`. `worktree` is present for a storage match
with a following component, or a git worktree match. `relpath` is relative to
`worktree` when present, otherwise to `location`; it is empty at that directory itself.
`root` always names the current registered root, and inapplicable fields are omitted.
A resolved row carries the project's `color` (`#rrggbb`) when its root is reachable and
its config sets one; a reachable config that cannot be read adds one warning naming the
project and leaves its rows resolved without `color`.

Per-item outcomes never fail a batch. Malformed UTF-8 stdin lines become `invalid`
