rows with replacement characters in `input` and decoding details; a stdin read error
adds an invalid diagnostic and stops reading, preserving earlier rows. Unavailable
relative-path bases also produce invalid rows. Only registry problems fail command
execution with the usual error envelope on stderr and exit 1.

### Completions

Bash and zsh complete subcommands, flags, `--status`/`--size`/`--sort`/`--color`
values, registered project prefixes, and task ids — `tasks show sci-4f<TAB>`. The id
candidates come from the project the command would actually act on, so `-C`,
`--project`, and a typed foreign prefix all steer them.

Bash, in `~/.bashrc`:

    source <(TASKS_COMPLETE=bash tasks)

Zsh, in `~/.zshrc`, **after** completion is initialized — the stub calls `compdef`, so
sourcing it before `compinit` fails with `command not found: compdef`:

    autoload -Uz compinit && compinit      # or your framework's own init
    source <(TASKS_COMPLETE=zsh tasks)

Under oh-my-zsh, prezto, or a plugin manager, the same rule applies: the stub goes after
that framework's initialization.

Re-source the stub or open a new shell after upgrading `tasks`; a running shell keeps the
function it loaded at startup. Fish, elvish, and powershell use the same mechanism with
their own syntax. `TASKS_COMPLETE=` or `TASKS_COMPLETE=0` disables completion.

### Color and layout

Color is off unless you ask for it. `--color auto|always|never`, or `TASKS_COLOR` with the
same three values, styles `--pretty` output only; JSON never carries escape sequences.
`auto` colors a stream only when that stream is a terminal, so putting `TASKS_COLOR=auto`
in a shell rc leaves piped and agent-run output plain. A non-empty `NO_COLOR` turns off
color selected through the environment, and an explicit `--color` overrides it.

Assign a persistent project color with an optional top-level key in `tasks/.config.toml`,
before any table headers:

```toml
prefix = "sci"
color = "#123456"
```

The value must be exactly `#RRGGBB` (either hex case); invalid values fail with a config
error. Change the value to change the color, or remove the key to restore existing styling.
Init/reinitialization and prefix rename preserve the setting. Pretty output paints a
project's name in that RGB in these places: the prefix in `projects`, `groups` and
`where`, and task ids and titles in every table view (`list`, `search`, `ready`, `tree`,
`prime`, `lanes`, `quiet`, `sample`) and in `show` and `next`, whose overview line, related
rows, lane and move pointers take the colour of the project each id belongs to. An id
paints a lighter shade of the colour (mixed 30% of the way to white in OKLab), so it reads
apart from the title beside it; the nearer a colour is to white, the less the two differ:

    TASKS_FORMAT=pretty tasks --color=always projects
    TASKS_FORMAT=pretty tasks --color=always list --all-projects

`claims` stays uncolored: it opens no checkout. Unassigned or unreachable projects keep their
existing styling; status, priority, dates, tags, and metadata keep their own roles.
Project colors obey the color controls above and never appear in stored task IDs. JSON
carries the color, whatever the color controls say, as lowercase `"color": "#rrggbb"` on
`projects` rows, on `where`'s `project`, and on `resolve`'s resolved rows, so another tool
can paint a project without reading its config. The key is omitted when the project sets
none or is unreachable; `resolve` also omits it, with a warning, when a config cannot be
read, where `projects` and `where` fail with the config error. Pretty `show`, `next` and
`groups` likewise leave another project's name uncolored, with a warning, when its config
cannot be read.

With color on, date columns fade by age: today in the terminal theme's cyan, older dates
toward a dimmed foreground, anything two years or more away the same. Priorities take the
theme's magenta: P0 bold, P1 full, then even steps down to a deeply dimmed foreground at
P4. The colors are read from the terminal itself (foreground, background and palette
slots 5 and 6), and only when stdout is a terminal, since a pager reading the same
terminal would race the query. For piped output, a terminal that does not answer, or ends of your own, set
`TASKS_PALETTE="fg=#rrggbb bg=#rrggbb cyan=#rrggbb magenta=#rrggbb"` (`magenta` may be
left out, which keeps priorities bold at P0 and P1); otherwise dates print plain,
priorities bold at P0 and P1, with one warning saying why. By default the colors come
from the terminal itself. `TASKS_THEME=default` instead uses the palette tasks ships
(`fg=#e5e3d7 bg=#13140d cyan=#00d7ff magenta=#d75fd7`), which sends no query and is
meant for dark backgrounds; a set `TASKS_PALETTE` still wins over it.
`TASKS_THEME=terminal` is the default behavior, spelled out.

`show` and `next` print their task in a reading layout: an `overview` section with one
aligned `key: value` row per set field, then the park, the description, related tasks,
attached files, and the notes, each under a ruled heading. Prose wraps at the terminal
width (or `COLUMNS`), capped at 100 columns, and stays unwrapped when piped. Fields take
the colors `list` gives them. The task file itself is `tasks/<id>.md`, and JSON output
carries every field.

### Agent skills

`skills/tasks/SKILL.md` teaches agents the session protocol. [Install](#1-install) puts
every skill at user level so they apply to every project; from a checkout of this repo
the recipe is:

    just install-skills

The recipe symlinks each `skills/*` directory into `~/.claude/skills` and
`~/.agents/skills` (the latter for other harnesses) and is idempotent: re-run it after
a pull adds a skill.

or per project, when a project needs to pin its own copy:

    mkdir -p <repo>/.claude/skills && cp -r skills/tasks <repo>/.claude/skills/tasks

`tasks init` warns when neither location has the skill.

`skills/curate/SKILL.md` is the maintenance pass: `/curate` samples open tasks and
refines them within fixed bounds.

`skills/scope/SKILL.md` is the deliberate idea review between capture and maintenance:
`/scope` turns a bounded cluster into supported next actions and handoffs.
[From idea to ready work](#from-idea-to-ready-work) gives the lifecycle it serves.

### Feedback

A report about a project's tooling goes to the project that owns it:

    tasks feedback --project <owner> "<one line about the tool>" --category <friction|gap|idea|positive> [-b "<detail>"]

The owner must be registered and opt in with a `[feedback]` table (`scope = "<what it
owns>"`) in its `tasks/.config.toml`; any other is refused with the list of those that
accept. The entry lands as an `idea` in the owner's registered checkout, tagged `feedback`,
the category, and `from:<your prefix>`, or `from:unregistered` when filed outside every
project. A repeat of the same one-liner in the same owner
appends a note to the open entry instead of creating a duplicate; `--recur <id>` and
`--new` settle an `ambiguous` result. The record is committed there when the owner sets
`[git] commit`. In the owner's repository, ideas tagged `feedback` without a triage note are unreviewed reports: read
each and redact project content with `tasks edit` (history keeps the original). This
repository is public.

### Adopting in an existing project

1. Keep historical docs in place. By default spec links accept docs/specs/,
   docs/designs/, docs/superpowers/specs/, and docs/superpowers/designs/; plan links
   accept docs/plans/ and docs/superpowers/plans/. If the project keeps them elsewhere,
   say so before `init`:

       mkdir -p tasks && cat > tasks/.config.toml <<'EOF'
       prefix = "sci"
       spec_dirs = ["design", "rfcs"]
       plan_dirs = ["planning"]
       EOF

   A configured list replaces the defaults. The roots are both the validation boundary
   and the search path for bare names, and they are project-level only so `tasks check`
   agrees on every machine.

   The same file may carry the project's tag dictionary, one line per tag with a
   specific meaning:

       [tags]
       testing = "Tests, gates, and CI."
       perf = "Speed or memory."

   `tasks tags` prints the meaning beside each tag, and `tasks check` warns
   `undefined_tag` for an open task carrying a tag the table does not define; a project
   without the table is not held to anything. A new metadata idea starts here as a tag
   plus an entry, and is promoted to a proper field only once it has earned validation
   and a JSON key — then the entry says so and `check` flushes the tag. Design:
   `docs/specs/2026-09-11-tag-dictionary-design.md`.
2. `tasks init --prefix <p>`.
3. Install the skill and mention it in the project's CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md.
4. Require `tasks prime` at session start and `tasks check` before completion. Add
   `tasks check` to automation once the binary has a pinned install source; never skip it
   conditionally when unavailable.

#### Record commits

Opt in per project in `tasks/.config.toml`:

    [git]
    commit = true

- Absent or false keeps manual commits; any other key in `[git]` is a config error.
- Each write commits its records and attachment changes, once per git working tree, plus anything the repository's pre-commit hook stages; staging by another git process while the commit runs can land in it.
- Configuration changes are not committed automatically: `init`, `rename`, `retire` and `unretire` leave `tasks/.config.toml` for you to commit, or for `tasks commit` to sweep.
- Subjects are `chore(tasks): <verb> <id>[ <id>…]`; `add` and `feedback` append the title, with the subject capped at 72 characters, with no trailer.
- `commit_unavailable:` means git is missing or the root is outside git; `commit_deferred:` means staged changes, detached HEAD or an in-progress git operation; `commit_failed:` means a git operation or hook failed.
- A successful write still exits 0 when its commit is skipped or fails; `cleanup needs attention:` means cleanup failed or the index could not be checked, so inspect the named paths and index.
- Clear the warning's cause, then run `tasks commit [--project <p>]` to recover or sweep every uncommitted file under `tasks/` into one commit; it ignores the switch and exits 1 when it cannot commit.
- Record commits preserve intermediate task history while code is in progress; code and record commits land on the task's branch before it merges.

## Bounded session summaries

For an opt-in JSON overview that fits a smaller response, use:

    tasks --json prime --summary

Ordinary `prime` keeps its complete output. Summary mode requires JSON; the explicit
`--json` overrides a valid `TASKS_FORMAT=pretty`. Upgrade the binary before adopting
the option rather than retrying an unsupported option as an unbounded read.

A successful summary is at most 12,288 UTF-8 stdout bytes including the final newline.
It initially includes up to five ready rows, five doing rows, five lanes, five roadmap
roots, three parks and three closeout goals. Roadmap descendants are omitted, while
the roots retain their child and open-descendant counts. If necessary, entire rows
are removed from roadmap, lanes, closeout, ready, parked, then doing until it fits.
Included rows, lane guidance, claims, paths and resume instructions are never clipped.
Counts, scheduling summaries, scope, warnings and halts remain complete.

The additional `summary` object discloses `byte_limit`, `complete` and `sections`.
Each section gives `total`, `shown`, `omitted` and, when rows are omitted,
`first_omitted`. Roadmap also gives `descendants_omitted`. These totals describe the
existing filtered view; `complete` does not establish that all projects were reachable.

`summary.full` is a JSON argument array for a fresh complete prime read through the
same executable, directory and scope. Execute its first member as the program and
the remaining members as arguments, keeping the same environment and capturing
stdout to a file; do not join the array into a shell command. Read large files in
bounded sections. In particular, recover omitted closeout invitations from full
prime's `closeout`; `list` and `tree` do not substitute for that invitation. Obtain
complete doing/parked data before planning parallel work or concluding no task can
be resumed. `start` still checks current ownership and gates.

If required metadata alone is too large, the command exits 1 with
`summary_too_large` on stderr and no stdout. Preserve the original invocation: rerun
that same binary, directory, scope and environment without `--summary`, capture full
stdout to a persistent file, and visibly report the summary failure and saved path.
A failed full capture remains an error; blank stdout does not mean there is no work.
Other errors should be handled directly. No warnings are dropped to force a fit.

The cap bounds bytes, rather than every consumer's token count, runtime or memory.
Reads are fresh, so claims and records can change between summary and recovery.
